summary: The draft is mostly well-cited, but three paragraphs need a few targeted citations: cost-based bribery and rule definitions in computational social choice, the Open LLM Leaderboard as the held-out data source, and the introduction's incentive claim about rankings.
missing_literatures: priced, swap and weighted bribery under Copeland, Borda and plurality
Goodhart's law and metric gaming in ML evaluation

rewrite_targets.reason: The Computational social choice paragraph says its problem is a 'continuous variant' of manipulation, bribery and margin-of-victory problems. The cited works are generic or about election attacks. The paragraph cites no work on cost-priced or swap bribery, or on Copeland, Borda and plurality specifically, which are the rules the planner treats with greedy heuristics. Reviewers will expect these closest comparators.
rewrite_targets.anchor_text: Our problem is a continuous variant: the ``voters'' are tasks, the intervention changes one candidate's scores
search_topics: priced bribery and swap bribery in elections
Copeland, Borda and plurality bribery and control complexity
bribery or manipulation under score-based or range voting with cost per voter

rewrite_targets.reason: All held-out results use Open LLM Leaderboard snapshots. The draft cites only the six component benchmarks and never the leaderboard itself, so the paper's main evaluation data source has no reference. HELM is cited through Liang et al., so only the Open LLM Leaderboard is missing.
rewrite_targets.anchor_text: The Open LLM Leaderboard aggregates six benchmarks
search_topics: Open LLM Leaderboard v2 (Hugging Face) description
Open LLM Leaderboard v1 or evaluation harness documentation

rewrite_targets.reason: The opening motivation ('Rankings influence adoption, publication and funding, so developers have an incentive to act on them') is stated as fact with no support. It is the premise of the whole question and has no Goodhart-style or leaderboard-culture reference.
rewrite_targets.anchor_text: Rankings influence adoption, publication and funding, so developers have an incentive to act on them
search_topics: Goodhart's law and metric gaming in machine learning benchmarks
benchmark culture and leaderboard incentives in ML
